purpose: Gap 2: the wave-2/prior research task was one run per client with no matched baseline, establishing neither a quality ranking nor a causal token difference. Gap 8: no matched execution establishes comparative model quality or causal provider savings across candidate clients. This check runs one frozen, bounded research task N=3 per client (`claude -p` vs `codex exec`) in counterbalanced order, blind-judges each of the 6 outputs against a rubric frozen before any run, and reports per-arm token/cost usage from each client's own native usage fields.
preregistered: Frozen before any arm ran, by file modification time: blueprints/gap-wave3-20260923/native-clients-research-task/task.md, rubric.json and run-order.json were written between 00:58:26 and 00:58:39 EDT, before run1_codex's first output at 00:59:19. rubric.json contains R1-R3 blind-judged 0/1 criteria plus a mechanical, non-judged R4 TIMESTAMP check, and run-order.json contains a seeded-random counterbalanced order, python random.seed(20260923) over ['claude']*3+['codex']*3, shuffled to codex,claude,codex,codex,claude,claude -- deliberately not blocked by client, unlike the wave-2 skill-arm-ab check where one arm always ran first and confounded cache-warmth with the arm variable. CORRECTION (fix round): 'committed to the worktree BEFORE any arm ran' was inaccurate and is retracted -- git only supports one commit for this whole evidence set (0da42cf, made at 01:17:57, after every run in this unit completed); freeze timing is established here by file modification time only, not by a git commit. Separately, the actual task-prompt.txt file passed to run-arm.sh's cat-the-prompt-file step was not preserved from the time of the six gap-2/8 runs: the task-prompt.txt now committed to the worktree has a modification time of 01:06:40, i.e. it was (re)written AFTER the last gap-2/8 output (run6_claude at 01:01:45), and its literal text differs cosmetically from task.md's markdown rendering of the 'verbatim' prompt (task.md wraps the date command and the TIMESTAMP line in backticks; the committed task-prompt.txt has no backticks and instead wraps the TIMESTAMP placeholder in double quotes). The prompt text's substance (the research question, the one-Bash-call instruction, the TIMESTAMP format) is unchanged between the two files, and all 6 raw outputs correctly produced a TIMESTAMP line and only one Bash call, consistent with either wording having been sent; but the exact bytes claude -p and codex exec received for the six gap-2/8 runs cannot be verified against the currently-committed task-prompt.txt with certainty, only inferred from task.md and the run outputs. 'Matched Bash-only tool scope' is also corrected below (see limitations): --allowedTools Bash only auto-approves Bash without prompting, it does not restrict which tools are available to the model, and in practice the claude -p arm ran with all 124 tools available in the invoking session, not a Bash-only tool set. Expected discriminating signal, stated before running: if one client's arm scores materially higher mean R1+R2+R3 with separated spread, that is evidence of a quality difference; if scores are indistinguishable, that is a valid null result to report, not evidence to discard. A second, short, distinct task was considered and explicitly not run (task.md), to keep the claude -p call budget (16 total for this unit, judge calls included) within bounds alongside gap 12's SDK-vs-CLI comparison.

result: All 6 research-task outputs (3 claude -p, 3 codex exec) independently converged on the same technique, Anthropic prompt caching, described coherently and with a concrete quantifiable figure (the 10%-of-base-price cache-read discount, ~90% saving) in every single run. The blind judge (client identity and TIMESTAMP stripped, packet order randomized) scored all 6 outputs 3/3 on R1/R2/R3 -- a clean ceiling effect. This is an honest, valid null result on quality for this specific bounded task: it does not show one client producing higher-quality output than the other, because the task was not hard enough to discriminate between them at medium effort. It does NOT establish that the two clients are equal in quality generally; it establishes only that on this one bounded research-recall task, both converged to essentially the same correct answer. CORRECTION (fix round): the tool-scope and context-attribution claims below were wrong in the original receipt and are corrected here from the raw system/init events. `--allowedTools Bash` only auto-approves Bash without prompting; per the installed SDK's own documentation (allowed_tools is 'auto-allowed without prompting'; restricting which tools exist requires the separate `tools` option, not exercised here), it does not restrict which tools are available to the model. In practice, per the raw system/init events, the claude -p research arm (run2_claude, run5_claude, run6_claude) and all 10 blind-judge calls ran with cwd=~/code/agent-lab (the coordinator's own checkout, not this unit's owned worktree) and permissionMode=bypassPermissions with 124 tools available, including WebFetch, WebSearch, and the serena/ai-memory/socraticode/jcodemunch MCP servers -- not a matched Bash-only tool set. By contrast, the separate gap-12 check's CLI arm (cli_run1/cli_run2/cli_resume) ran in this unit's own worktree with 47 tools available. So 'matched tool scope' held only because the prompt explicitly instructed 'do not use any tool other than Bash' and each of the 6 runs happened to comply (every run made exactly one Bash `date` call and no web/MCP calls, confirmed from the raw command_execution/tool_use events, so the answer text itself was not contaminated by the wider tool availability) -- it was not enforced by the harness, and the gap-12 CLI arm's 47-tool, worktree-scoped run is not directly comparable to this check's own 124-tool, coordinator-checkout claude -p run despite sharing the same prompt text. Token usage, which the two clients report in structurally different, non-directly-comparable schemas, differed substantially: claude -p's per-turn 'new' input_tokens field stayed at 4 (the ~80k-token system-prompt/tool-definition prefix is charged separately as cache_creation_input_tokens/cache_read_input_tokens, averaging ~29k creation + ~52k read per call), while codex exec's single 'input_tokens' field already reports the full per-turn context inclusive of its own cached_input_tokens sub-component, averaging ~49.6k per call with a smaller, ~29.2k cached component. Comparing claude's 'input_tokens: 4' against codex's 'input_tokens: ~49.6k' at face value would be a schema-mismatch artifact, not a real ~12,000x difference; the fairer combined-context figures (claude ~4 + ~29k + ~52k =~81.2k mean; codex ~49.6k mean) still show claude's total per-turn context transfer as roughly 1.6x codex's on this task. CORRECTION (fix round): the original receipt attributed this ~81k-token claude-side context to 'this repository's own CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md instruction files being loaded' -- that claim is retracted. The claude -p arm ran with cwd=~/code/agent-lab, so any project-instruction files loaded were that repository's, not this evidence receipt's own repository; more importantly, the dominant confound is the 124 available tool schemas (versus codex exec's much smaller native shell-only toolset), not specifically CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md instruction text, and this receipt did not isolate the two. The claude/codex context gap on this task remains confounded by mismatched tool-schema counts and invoking-directory system-prompt content, not established as a client-intrinsic property. Output length differed too: claude's mean output_tokens (588) exceeded codex's mean output_tokens (315) by roughly 1.9x, while codex additionally reports reasoning_output_tokens (mean 124) as a distinct sub-field claude does not expose the same way (claude's thinking tokens are folded into output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens, itself a component of the total output_tokens already counted). Only claude -p exposes a native total_cost_usd figure (mean $0.2548 per research call at this account's list pricing, each from an independent fresh session_id so this mean is not a cumulative-cost artifact); codex exec's native usage event carries no cost field on this host/config, so no direct dollar comparison is possible from native usage alone -- this is itself evidence that a same-currency cost comparison across these two clients is not available from native tooling without an external, independently-priced conversion, which this unit did not attempt.

verdict_impact.explanation: Advances gap 2 and gap 8 by replacing the prior single-run-per-client, no-baseline evidence with an N=3-per-client, counterbalanced-order, blind-judged comparison and native per-arm usage; the counterbalanced order, frozen rubric, and blind stripped-identity judging are real methodological improvements over the wave-2 baseline and stand. Does not fully settle either gap, and settles it less cleanly than the original write-up claimed: quality is a genuine ceiling-effect null result on this one bounded task (not evidence of equal quality generally, and not evidence the task was well-chosen to discriminate quality -- a harder or more open-ended task might separate the arms); the token/cost comparison is confounded by the two clients' structurally different usage-reporting schemas and by mismatched tool-schema counts (124 tools available to claude -p vs codex exec's much smaller native toolset), not specifically by this repository's own instruction files as the original write-up claimed; and (fix round correction) the preregistered 'matched Bash-only tool scope' was not actually enforced -- the claude -p arm ran with all 124 tools auto-approved in the coordinator's own checkout, and only complied with Bash-only in practice because the model followed the prompt's instruction, not because the harness restricted it. Labeled diagnostic per the unit's own instruction, not universal.

limitations: N=3 per arm is small; a single frozen task with a 3-point ceiling-prone rubric could not discriminate quality between the two clients on this occasion (all 6 outputs scored 3/3). A harder task, a finer-grained rubric, or more trials might reveal a difference this design cannot detect.

Only one frozen task was run (the optional second task was explicitly skipped to conserve this unit's shared 16-call claude -p budget across gap 2/8 and gap 12); this cannot establish a general ranking across task types.

CORRECTION (fix round): the claude -p research arm (run2_claude, run5_claude, run6_claude) and all 10 blind-judge calls in this unit actually ran with cwd=~/code/agent-lab and permissionMode=bypassPermissions with 124 tools available (including WebFetch, WebSearch, and MCP servers), not the intended worktree with a restricted Bash-only tool set, because `--allowedTools Bash` only auto-approves Bash rather than removing other tools from availability. Each of the 6 runs happened to comply with the prompt's 'Bash only' instruction (one `date` call each, no web/MCP calls observed in the raw events), so the answer text itself is not known to be contaminated, but 'matched tool scope' was not actually enforced, and the preregistered claim that it was is retracted.

The two clients report native usage in structurally different, non-directly-comparable schemas (see result); the 'combined context' figures computed here are the best available same-unit comparison but remain confounded by the large tool-schema count (124 tools) loaded for the claude -p arm's invoking session relative to codex exec's much smaller native toolset -- not, as the original receipt claimed, by this repository's own CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md files specifically (that attribution was wrong: the claude -p arm ran in a different repository's checkout, ~/code/agent-lab, not this one).

CORRECTION (fix round): the preregistration files (task.md, rubric.json, run-order.json, run-arm.sh) were frozen before any arm ran by file modification time (00:58:26-00:58:56, before run1_codex at 00:59:19), but were only committed to git afterward in a single commit (0da42cf, 01:17:57) alongside every other file in this unit's evidence set -- git commit time does not establish freeze timing here, file mtime does. Separately, the exact task-prompt.txt bytes passed to run-arm.sh during the six gap-2/8 runs were not preserved: the currently-committed task-prompt.txt has a modification time of 01:06:40, after the last gap-2/8 output (run6_claude, 01:01:45), and differs cosmetically from task.md's markdown rendering of the prompt (task.md uses backticks around the date command and the TIMESTAMP line; the committed task-prompt.txt has no backticks and instead quotes the TIMESTAMP placeholder). The prompt's substance is unchanged and all 6 outputs behaved consistently with either wording, but the literal bytes actually sent cannot be independently re-verified from the current worktree state.

CORRECTION (fix round): judge-prompt-template.txt (written at 01:02:31, after all six gap-2/8 outputs already existed at 00:59:19-01:01:45) reproduces rubric.json's R1-R3 criteria text but drops rubric.json R1's attribution-leniency clause ('a named technique/provider/system is acceptable even if the exact provider attribution cannot be independently re-verified by the judge in this sealed context'). All 6 outputs still scored R1=1, so this omission is not known to have changed any score in this run, but the judge prompt actually sent was not a verbatim copy of the frozen rubric.

No dollar-cost comparison is possible: codex exec's native usage event carries no cost field on this host/config; only claude -p's total_cost_usd is available, and it reflects this account's list pricing, not necessarily a directly comparable rate to any codex/OpenAI billing.

The blind judge is itself a single claude -p call per output (not cross-checked by a second independent judge or human rater); a judge systematically biased toward or against a particular writing style could affect all 6 scores in the same direction without being detected by this design, though the ceiling effect here makes that concern moot for this run.

Order was counterbalanced but not fully Latin-square balanced across all 6! possible orderings; a single seeded-random order was used, recorded and followed exactly, but residual cache-state or time-of-day effects across the ~3-minute run window cannot be fully ruled out.

This receipt reports the sum of the 3-run research-arm usage per client in model_calls; the 6 individual blind-judge calls' usage is not summed into a combined total (to avoid conflating judge-call cost with research-call cost) and is only available per-call in the out-of-repo raw artifacts referenced below.

The codex exec model_calls entry names 'gpt-6-astra' from this host's ~/.codex/config.toml default, not from a per-call model field in the --json event stream (the stream does not echo one); the actual resolved model for these 3 calls is read from config, not independently confirmed per call.
